item.title: Amazon's Fire Phone Flop: The $170 Million Failure Behind Alexa
item.description:
In 2014 Amazon took a $170 million write-down on the Fire Phone, a gadget almost nobody wanted. Two weeks later the same lab unveiled the Echo. Here's why the phone flopped, how Amazon handled the failure, and how small businesses can fail cheaply and keep the lessons. #Amazon #FirePhone #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Fail cheaply, protect the people who took the bet, and carry the lessons into the next one.

item.title: Southwest's 10-Minute Turn: How Selling a Plane Built a Strategy
item.description:
In 1972 Southwest Airlines was so short of cash it had to sell one of its four jets, but it refused to cut a single flight. The answer was the ten-minute turn, and it shaped the airline for fifty years. Here's how one hard limit became a strategy, and how small businesses can do the same. #SouthwestAirlines #Strategy #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: A constraint you can't escape can become your whole strategy, if you design everything around it and keep checking it still fits.

item.title: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera in 1975. Why It Still Went Bankrupt
item.description:
In 1975 a young Kodak engineer built the world's first digital camera. Kodak patented it, kept it quiet, and in 2012 filed for bankruptcy anyway. Here's what really went wrong, and how small businesses can avoid protecting yesterday's profits. #Kodak #Innovation #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Don't protect today's profits from the thing that will replace them; if someone is going to eat your business, make sure it's you.

item.title: Apple's 1997 Comeback: Why Steve Jobs Cut 70% of Its Products
item.description:
In 1997 Apple was losing about a billion dollars a year and a rival CEO said it should shut down. Steve Jobs drew four boxes on a whiteboard and killed most of the product line. Here's how saying no saved Apple, and how to use the same move in a small business. #Apple #SteveJobs #BusinessLessons

Today's lesson: Focus means saying no to good ideas, not just bad ones, so your best few can win.

item.title: Coca-Cola's New Coke Disaster: Why Taste Tests Lied in 1985
item.description:
In 1985 Coca-Cola ran nearly two hundred thousand taste tests, found a formula people liked better, and replaced the most famous drink on Earth. Seventy-nine days later the original was back on shelves. Here's what the research missed, why the comeback worked, and how to change your own product without losing the customers who love it. #business #cocacola #entrepreneurship

Today's lesson: Customers don't just buy what tastes best; they buy what they feel belongs to them, so ask what they'd lose, not only what they prefer.

item.title: Netflix's Qwikster Mistake: Right Strategy, Wrong Way to Do It
item.description:
In 2011 Netflix knew streaming was the future. Then it hiked prices 60% and tried to split its DVD service into a new brand called Qwikster, lost 800,000 US subscribers in one quarter, and reversed course in about three weeks. What went wrong, what Netflix got right, and how to change your own business without losing the people who pay you. #business #netflix #entrepreneurship

Today's lesson: Being right about the future is not enough: don't make your customers pay for your transition.
